title: Sacagawea Finds Her Brother
text:
Sacagawea was a Lemhi Shoshone girl captured by a Hidatsa raiding party around 1800 and taken far east to the villages on the Missouri River. There she became one of the wives of a French Canadian trader, Toussaint Charbonneau. In 1804 the American explorers Meriwether Lewis and William Clark hired Charbonneau as an interpreter, partly because Sacagawea could speak Shoshone. She joined the expedition in April 1805 with her infant son on her back.

The explorers needed horses to cross the Rocky Mountains, and the Shoshone were the people who had them. In August 1805, near the Continental Divide, Lewis met a Shoshone band and persuaded its chief, Cameahwait, to come back with him to meet Clark's party. On 17 August, as they met, Sacagawea began to dance and suck her fingers, a sign that these were her own people. During the council that followed she recognized Cameahwait as her brother. The account Nicholas Biddle later prepared from the expedition's records says she jumped up, ran to him, threw her blanket over him and wept.

The reunion helped the expedition get the horses and the guide it needed. Lewis wrote that the meeting was very affecting. Sacagawea learned that most of her family had died, though she found the son of a sister, whom she adopted. Then she continued west with the expedition to the Pacific.
lesson: Family ties can open doors that no amount of negotiation can. Keeping connection with where we came from can matter at the moment we least expect.
people: Sacagawea, Cameahwait, Meriwether Lewis, William Clark
location: Camp Fortunate, near Lemhi Pass, Montana, USA
source: The Journals of the Lewis and Clark Expedition, entries for 17 August 1805; Nicholas Biddle, History of the Expedition under the Command of Captains Lewis and Clark (1814)
caveat: Accounts disagree on details of Sacagawea's later life, but the reunion itself is recorded in the expedition journals.
